tabs.Scenario: A 72-year-old is admitted with pneumonia. Initial data: T 39.1 C, HR 124/min, RR 30/min, BP 92/54 mmHg, SpO2 90% on room air, new confusion and urine output 20 mL/hr.
A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, deep respirations and dehydration. Glucose 610 mg/dL, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, positive ketones, K 5.6 mEq/L.
A client one hour after vaginal birth saturates a pad rapidly. The uterus is boggy and above the umbilicus; HR 122/min, BP 88/50 mmHg.
A 58-year-old on postoperative day 2 suddenly reports sharp chest pain and dyspnea. HR 128/min, RR 32/min, SpO2 84%, BP 94/58 mmHg.

items.stem: A client with suspected infection has T 39.2 C, HR 128/min, RR 30/min, BP 86/48 mmHg, new confusion, and urine output 15 mL/hr. Which finding most strongly indicates impaired perfusion?
items.rationale: Marked oliguria is an important cue of reduced renal perfusion in a hemodynamically unstable client.

items.stem: Blood cultures have been obtained from a client with sepsis and prescriptions include IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and isotonic crystalloid. Which action is the priority?
options: Begin the prescribed time-sensitive sepsis treatment promptly
Restrict fluids until urine culture results
Give an antipyretic before other treatment
items.rationale: Sepsis requires prompt treatment of infection and restoration of perfusion; therapy should not wait for final culture results.

items.stem: After a large GI bleed, a client is pale and cool with HR 132/min, BP 78/44 mmHg, weak pulses and delayed capillary refill. Which type of shock is most consistent with these cues?
items.rationale: Acute blood loss reduces circulating intravascular volume, producing hypovolemic shock.

items.stem: A client after a large MI has crackles, JVD, cool skin and hypotension. Which prescription should the nurse question if it is ordered as a rapid large-volume intervention?
options: Large rapid isotonic fluid bolus without reassessment
items.rationale: Cardiogenic shock reflects pump failure; indiscriminate large rapid fluid loading can worsen pulmonary congestion.

items.stem: A postoperative client suddenly develops dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, HR 122/min and oxygen saturation 86%. Which complication should the nurse suspect first?
items.rationale: Sudden hypoxemia, tachycardia and pleuritic chest pain after surgery are classic warning cues for pulmonary embolism.

items.stem: A client with a chest tube becomes acutely dyspneic. The nurse finds the tubing disconnected from the drainage system. What should the nurse do first?
options: Clamp the chest tube near the client for the remainder of the shift
Re-establish the drainage system connection using aseptic technique and assess the client
Turn the client onto the affected side and leave the tube disconnected
items.rationale: A disconnected system can allow air entry and loss of drainage; restore the closed system promptly while assessing respiratory status.

items.stem: A client with severe pneumonia has worsening hypoxemia despite supplemental oxygen and bilateral diffuse infiltrates. Which complication is the priority concern?
items.rationale: Refractory hypoxemia with diffuse bilateral pulmonary involvement after a major insult is consistent with ARDS.

items.stem: After treatment for an acute asthma exacerbation, which finding best indicates improvement?
options: Ability to speak in full sentences with improved air movement
items.rationale: Improved ventilation is reflected by better air movement, reduced work of breathing and ability to speak comfortably.

items.stem: Which intervention is most appropriate for a client with COPD who becomes short of breath during activity?
options: Teach pursed-lip breathing and pace activities
Keep the client flat in bed
items.rationale: Pursed-lip breathing prolongs exhalation and activity pacing reduces ventilatory demand.

items.stem: ABG results are pH 7.30, PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 25 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these values?
items.rationale: The pH is acidotic and PaCO2 is elevated while bicarbonate is near normal, indicating uncompensated respiratory acidosis.

items.stem: Which assessment is the most sensitive routine indicator of changing fluid volume in a client with heart failure?
items.rationale: Daily weight trends are a sensitive practical measure of fluid gain or loss.

items.stem: A client reports crushing substernal chest pressure with diaphoresis and nausea. Which nursing action is the priority?
options: Obtain rapid assessment, ECG and initiate the acute chest-pain protocol
Delay assessment until pain has lasted 30 minutes
items.rationale: Possible acute coronary syndrome requires immediate assessment and time-sensitive evaluation/treatment.

items.stem: A client after cardiac surgery develops hypotension, JVD and muffled heart sounds. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: Hypotension, jugular venous distention and muffled heart sounds are classic cues associated with cardiac tamponade.

items.stem: The monitor shows ventricular tachycardia. The client is unresponsive and has no palpable pulse. What should the nurse do first?
options: Begin CPR and activate the resuscitation response
Obtain a routine 12-lead ECG before intervening
Place the client in Trendelenburg and reassess in 30 minutes
items.rationale: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia is cardiac arrest; immediate high-quality CPR and resuscitation are required.

items.stem: Which statement by a client with hypertension indicates correct understanding of home management?
options: I will stop my medicine when my blood pressure is normal
I will monitor my blood pressure and take medicines as prescribed even when I feel well
I should double every dose if one reading is high
Exercise is unsafe for everyone with hypertension
items.rationale: Hypertension is often asymptomatic; adherence and monitoring remain important even when readings improve.

items.stem: A client suddenly develops facial droop, unilateral arm weakness and difficulty speaking. What is the priority nursing action?
options: Activate the stroke response and establish the time last known well
Give an IM injection for pain
items.rationale: Stroke care is time-sensitive; rapid activation and accurate last-known-well time are essential.

items.stem: Which intervention is appropriate for a client with increased intracranial pressure?
options: Keep head and neck in neutral alignment with the head of bed elevated as prescribed
Cluster all care with repeated Valsalva maneuvers
Place the client flat with hips sharply flexed
items.rationale: Neutral alignment and appropriate head elevation promote venous drainage and help limit further ICP elevation.

items.stem: A hospitalized client begins a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Protect the head, clear nearby hazards, and turn the client to the side when possible
Force oral medication between the teeth
items.rationale: During a seizure, protect from injury and support airway drainage; do not restrain or place objects in the mouth.

items.stem: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury develops a pounding headache, flushing above the lesion and BP 210/110 mmHg. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: Severe hypertension with headache and flushing in a client with a high spinal cord lesion is characteristic of autonomic dysreflexia.

items.stem: A client is admitted with suspected bacterial meningitis. Which infection-control action is most appropriate initially?
options: Use only standard precautions regardless of organism
Place the client in a positive-pressure room
Delay precautions until culture results are final
items.rationale: Suspected bacterial meningitis requires prompt appropriate transmission-based precautions while the cause is clarified.

items.stem: A client with DKA has glucose 620 mg/dL, K 5.4 mEq/L, BP 88/52 mmHg and dry mucous membranes. Which intervention is generally the initial priority?
options: Begin prescribed isotonic IV fluid replacement
Administer sodium bicarbonate routinely before fluids
items.rationale: Severe dehydration and poor perfusion are major immediate problems in DKA; isotonic fluid resuscitation is a key initial intervention.

items.stem: During treatment of DKA, which finding requires especially close monitoring because therapy can rapidly change it?
items.rationale: Insulin and correction of acidosis shift potassium into cells, so serum potassium can fall rapidly during DKA treatment.

items.stem: An older adult with type 2 diabetes has glucose 980 mg/dL, profound dehydration, altered mental status and minimal ketones. Which condition is most likely?
items.rationale: Extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolar dehydration and neurologic changes with little ketosis are characteristic of HHS.

items.stem: A conscious client taking insulin is shaky and diaphoretic; bedside glucose is 52 mg/dL and the client can swallow safely. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give a fast-acting carbohydrate according to protocol
items.rationale: A conscious client with symptomatic hypoglycemia who can swallow should receive prompt fast-acting carbohydrate.

items.stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with SIADH?
options: Low serum sodium with concentrated urine
High serum sodium with very dilute urine
items.rationale: Excess ADH promotes water retention, dilutional hyponatremia and inappropriately concentrated urine.

items.stem: Which finding is most consistent with diabetes insipidus?
options: Large volumes of dilute urine and rising serum sodium
items.rationale: Deficient ADH effect causes inability to concentrate urine, producing polyuria, dehydration and possible hypernatremia.

items.stem: Which findings are expected with primary adrenal insufficiency?
items.rationale: Loss of adrenal cortical hormones can cause hypotension, sodium loss and hyperkalemia.

items.stem: A client with hyperthyroidism develops fever 40 C, severe tachycardia and agitation. What should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: High fever, marked tachycardia and CNS excitation in hyperthyroidism are emergency cues for thyroid storm.

items.stem: A client with AKI has potassium 6.4 mEq/L and peaked T waves. Which problem is the immediate priority?
items.rationale: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes threatens cardiac conduction and requires urgent treatment.

items.stem: Before using an arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis, what should the nurse assess?
options: Presence of a thrill and bruit
items.rationale: A palpable thrill and audible bruit indicate blood flow through the vascular access.

items.stem: A client receiving peritoneal dialysis has cloudy effluent and abdominal pain. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: Cloudy dialysate with abdominal pain is a warning sign of peritonitis and requires prompt evaluation.

items.stem: A client with cirrhosis becomes confused and develops asterixis. Which complication is most likely?
items.rationale: Altered cognition and asterixis in advanced liver disease are classic cues of hepatic encephalopathy.

items.stem: A client has hematemesis, HR 126/min and BP 82/46 mmHg. Which action is the priority?
options: Support airway/circulation and obtain large-bore IV access for resuscitation
Delay intervention until hemoglobin is repeated tomorrow
items.rationale: An unstable GI bleed threatens circulation and requires immediate ABC-focused resuscitation.

items.stem: Which assessment is most consistent with acute pancreatitis?
options: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea
items.rationale: Acute pancreatitis commonly causes severe upper abdominal/epigastric pain that may radiate to the back.

items.stem: Which finding is most concerning for bowel obstruction?
options: Abdominal distention, vomiting and inability to pass stool or flatus
items.rationale: Distention, vomiting and obstipation are key obstruction cues.

items.stem: A client is admitted with vaso-occlusive sickle cell pain. Which interventions are appropriate?
options: Assess pain, support hydration as prescribed, give analgesia, and evaluate oxygenation
Apply ice directly to painful areas for prolonged periods
Withhold prescribed analgesics until pain becomes unbearable
items.rationale: Management centers on pain control, hydration when appropriate, oxygenation assessment and treatment of triggers/complications.

items.stem: A critically ill client has oozing from IV sites, petechiae, prolonged coagulation tests and falling platelets. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: Simultaneous abnormal clotting and bleeding with thrombocytopenia in critical illness is consistent with DIC.

items.stem: Which instruction is most appropriate for a client with severe neutropenia?
options: Report fever promptly and avoid exposure to people who are ill
items.rationale: With severe neutropenia, infection can progress rapidly; fever requires prompt reporting and infection exposure should be minimized.

items.stem: Fifteen minutes after a blood transfusion begins, a client develops chills, dyspnea and back pain. What should the nurse do first?
options: Stop the transfusion and maintain IV access with appropriate compatible fluid per protocol
Discard the blood bag immediately before notifying anyone
items.rationale: A suspected transfusion reaction requires immediate cessation of the blood product while maintaining IV access and initiating the facility reaction protocol.

items.stem: A client receiving heparin develops a major platelet decline and new thrombosis. Which adverse effect should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: A substantial platelet fall with thrombosis during heparin exposure is concerning for HIT.

items.stem: A client taking digoxin reports nausea and new visual color changes and has bradycardia. What should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: GI symptoms, visual disturbances and bradyarrhythmias are important toxicity cues with digoxin.

items.stem: A postoperative client who received an opioid is difficult to arouse, RR 6/min and oxygen saturation is falling. What is the priority?
options: Support ventilation and administer naloxone as prescribed
items.rationale: Severe opioid-induced respiratory depression is an airway/breathing emergency; ventilatory support and opioid reversal may be required.

items.stem: The nurse notices that a medication dose appears unusually high compared with the client’s usual prescription. What is the safest action?
options: Hold the dose and clarify the prescription before administration
Administer it because it is in the electronic record
Ask the client to decide whether the dose is safe
items.rationale: A questionable prescription should be verified before administration to prevent medication error.

items.stem: When preparing compatible regular and NPH insulin in the same syringe, which sequence is appropriate?
options: Draw up clear regular insulin before cloudy NPH insulin
Draw cloudy NPH before clear regular insulin
items.rationale: For compatible regular and NPH insulin, clear regular insulin is drawn before cloudy NPH to reduce contamination of regular insulin.

items.stem: A client receiving magnesium sulfate has RR 9/min, absent deep tendon reflexes and decreasing urine output. What should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: Respiratory depression, loss of reflexes and reduced renal clearance are major toxicity cues.

items.stem: A pregnant client with severe preeclampsia reports persistent severe headache and visual changes. What is the priority?
options: Treat as signs of severe disease and notify/act promptly according to the obstetric plan
Reassure that these are normal pregnancy findings
Delay reassessment until the next day
items.rationale: Neurologic symptoms can signal severe preeclampsia and increased seizure risk, requiring prompt evaluation and management.

items.stem: The fetal monitor shows recurrent late decelerations. What do these decelerations most commonly suggest?
items.rationale: Late decelerations are associated with reduced uteroplacental oxygen exchange.

items.stem: Recurrent variable decelerations appear during labor. Which cause should the nurse consider first?
items.rationale: Variable decelerations are classically associated with intermittent umbilical cord compression.

items.stem: One hour after birth, a client has heavy vaginal bleeding and a boggy uterus. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Massage the uterine fundus and initiate the hemorrhage response as indicated
Apply an ice pack to the calf
items.rationale: A boggy uterus suggests uterine atony; fundal massage is an immediate nursing action while hemorrhage management proceeds.

items.stem: Which newborn finding requires immediate evaluation?
options: Irregular respirations with brief pauses and no color change
items.rationale: Central cyanosis can indicate inadequate oxygenation and requires prompt assessment.

items.stem: A child has high fever, drooling, muffled voice and sits leaning forward. Which action is safest?
options: Keep the child calm and prepare for expert airway management
Use a tongue depressor to inspect the throat
Force the child to lie flat
Obtain a throat swab before addressing the airway
items.rationale: Possible epiglottitis is an airway emergency; avoid upsetting the child or manipulating the throat because obstruction can worsen.

items.stem: Which assessment is most consistent with croup?
options: Drooling with tripod positioning and no cough
items.rationale: Croup commonly presents with a barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor.

items.stem: A child with Kawasaki disease is being monitored primarily for which serious complication?
items.rationale: Kawasaki disease can affect coronary arteries, so cardiac monitoring/follow-up is central.

items.stem: An infant has episodic severe abdominal pain, draws the knees to the chest, and later passes red mucus-like stool. Which condition is most likely?
items.rationale: Intermittent colicky pain with characteristic bloody mucus stool is a classic intussusception pattern.

items.stem: A young infant has progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting after feeds and remains hungry afterward. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
items.rationale: Projectile nonbilious vomiting with persistent hunger is characteristic of pyloric outlet obstruction.

items.stem: A client says, "I have a gun at home and plan to use it tonight." What is the nurse’s priority response?
options: Initiate immediate suicide-safety precautions and obtain urgent evaluation
Promise to keep the statement secret
Leave the client alone to reduce stimulation
Discuss long-term career goals before addressing safety
items.rationale: A specific plan with access to lethal means indicates acute suicide risk; immediate safety measures take priority.

items.stem: A grieving client says, "I cannot believe this happened." Which response is most therapeutic?
options: "Tell me what feels hardest for you right now."
"At least your family member lived a long life."
items.rationale: An open invitation to express feelings acknowledges the client’s experience without minimizing or giving false reassurance.

items.stem: A client says, "The voices are telling me to hurt myself." What should the nurse do first?
options: Assess the content, intent, ability to resist, and immediate safety risk
Tell the client the voices are real
Leave the client alone until the voices stop
items.rationale: Command hallucinations require immediate focused safety assessment and protective intervention as needed.

items.stem: Which intervention is most appropriate for a client with acute mania who cannot sit through meals?
options: Offer portable high-calorie nutritious foods and fluids while maintaining a low-stimulation environment
Insist on long formal group meals
items.rationale: Acute mania increases activity and distractibility; simple portable nutrition and reduced stimulation support safety and intake.

items.stem: Which task is most appropriate for the RN to delegate to trained UAP for a stable client?
options: Teach a newly diagnosed client how to self-inject insulin
items.rationale: Routine data collection on a stable client can be delegated; assessment, planning and initial teaching remain RN responsibilities.

items.stem: Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with new stridor after neck surgery
A client requesting a routine stool softener
A stable client awaiting discharge papers
A client with chronic knee pain rated 3/10
items.rationale: New stridor signals potential airway obstruction and takes priority under ABC principles.

items.stem: After caring for a client with suspected C. difficile diarrhea, which hand-hygiene approach is most appropriate when leaving the room?
options: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water
Wear the same gloves to the next room
Skip hand hygiene if gloves were worn
items.rationale: Soap-and-water handwashing is important after C. difficile exposure because spores are not reliably removed by alcohol hand rub alone.

items.stem: Which intervention best helps prevent pressure injury in an immobile client?
options: Regularly reposition, offload pressure, manage moisture, and optimize nutrition
Use donut-shaped rings under the sacrum routinely
Keep damp linens in place to reduce friction
items.rationale: Pressure redistribution, moisture control, skin surveillance and adequate nutrition are core prevention strategies.

items.stem: Which intervention is appropriate for a hospitalized client at high risk for falls?
options: Keep needed items within reach, use appropriate assistance, and maintain a clutter-free environment
Raise all four side rails and treat them as a substitute for observation
Encourage the client to walk alone at night
Place frequently used items on a high shelf
items.rationale: Accessible items, assisted mobility and environmental safety reduce fall risk without relying on restrictive measures.

items.stem: During mass-casualty triage, which client is generally tagged for immediate treatment?
options: A client with compromised breathing/perfusion who is likely to survive with rapid intervention
A walking client with a minor wrist sprain
A client with superficial abrasions only
A client with injuries incompatible with survival despite available resources
items.rationale: Disaster triage prioritizes immediate resources for life-threatening but potentially survivable problems.

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated client meets the facility’s referral triggers for possible organ donation. What is the nurse’s appropriate action?
options: Make the required referral to the designated organ procurement organization according to policy
Ask the family for organ consent before any referral
Promise the family that donation will occur
Change the goals of care without an authorized decision
items.rationale: The clinical team follows referral policy; trained organ-procurement personnel coordinate eligibility and donation discussions.

items.stem: A client with major burns has soot around the mouth, hoarseness and facial burns. What is the priority concern?
items.rationale: Inhalation injury can cause rapidly progressive airway edema; airway assessment and early expert management are priorities.

items.stem: A trauma client is unconscious and has snoring respirations after a high-speed collision. What is the priority?
options: Open and protect the airway while maintaining cervical spine precautions
Delay airway intervention until imaging is complete
items.rationale: Airway is the first trauma priority, with cervical spine protection when injury is possible.

items.stem: Which findings can indicate worsening tissue hypoperfusion in sepsis?
options: Warm dry skin alone without other changes
items.rationale: Altered mentation, oliguria and hypotension are important signs of impaired perfusion.

items.stem: Which findings are concerning for severe preeclampsia?
items.rationale: Neurologic symptoms, severe hypertension and upper abdominal pain can signal severe disease.

items.stem: Which actions are appropriate for a client with severe neutropenia?
items.rationale: Infection prevention and rapid response to fever are central; rectal procedures can injure mucosa and introduce infection.

items.stem: Which findings can indicate worsening heart failure?
items.rationale: Fluid retention and pulmonary/systemic congestion commonly cause weight gain, orthopnea, crackles and edema.

items.stem: Which findings suggest magnesium sulfate toxicity?
items.rationale: Respiratory depression and loss of reflexes are toxicity signs; oliguria increases risk because magnesium is renally cleared.

items.stem: The prescription is for 125 mg of a medication. The available concentration is 250 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should the nurse administer? (Round to one decimal place if needed.)
items.rationale: Use desired/have x volume: 125/250 x 5 = 2.5 mL.

items.stem: Which findings are most concerning for systemic deterioration?
options: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, confusion and oliguria
items.rationale: The combined abnormal vital signs, altered mentation and low urine output suggest systemic illness with impaired perfusion.

items.stem: Which problem best explains the client’s hypotension, confusion and oliguria?
options: Impaired tissue perfusion associated with sepsis
items.rationale: The pattern links infection with circulatory dysfunction and organ hypoperfusion.

items.stem: Which hypothesis is highest priority?
items.rationale: Hemodynamic instability and organ dysfunction are immediately life-threatening.

items.stem: Which plan best addresses the priority problem?
options: Prompt sepsis treatment, perfusion support, oxygenation assessment and close reassessment
Delay treatment until all cultures finalize
Restrict all fluids regardless of hemodynamics
Focus only on fever comfort measures
items.rationale: Management targets infection, oxygenation and perfusion while monitoring response.

items.stem: Blood cultures are obtained. Which action should occur next without unnecessary delay?
options: Initiate prescribed antibiotics and resuscitative therapy
Ambulate the client in the hallway
items.rationale: Time-sensitive therapy should follow appropriate cultures without waiting for final results.

items.stem: Which change best indicates improving perfusion?
options: MAP and mentation improve and urine output rises
items.rationale: Improving blood pressure, cognition and urine output indicate better organ perfusion.

items.stem: Which data support DKA?
options: Hyperglycemia, ketones, low bicarbonate and deep respirations
items.rationale: Hyperglycemia, ketosis and metabolic acidosis with compensatory respirations support DKA.

items.stem: Why can the initial serum potassium be elevated despite total-body potassium depletion?
options: Acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells while osmotic diuresis causes total losses
The kidneys always retain all potassium in DKA
The client has eaten too much potassium only
items.rationale: Extracellular shifts can raise measured potassium even while urinary losses deplete total-body stores.

items.stem: Which immediate problem is highest priority?
items.rationale: Circulatory volume depletion and metabolic abnormalities require immediate stabilization.

items.stem: Which initial plan is appropriate?
options: Isotonic fluids, insulin per protocol, electrolyte monitoring/replacement and frequent reassessment
Fluid restriction and no laboratory monitoring
Routine bicarbonate for every client before fluids
items.rationale: DKA treatment requires fluids, insulin and close electrolyte/clinical monitoring.

items.stem: After fluids are started and insulin therapy begins, which laboratory value needs especially close serial monitoring?
items.rationale: Insulin and correction of acidosis can rapidly lower serum potassium.

items.stem: Which findings suggest DKA is resolving?
options: Improving acidosis/anion gap, hydration and mental status
Falling blood pressure and urine output
items.rationale: Resolution is reflected by correction of metabolic acidosis and improved clinical perfusion/hydration.

items.stem: Which cues require immediate attention?
options: Heavy bleeding, boggy uterus, tachycardia and hypotension
items.rationale: Heavy bleeding with uterine atony and hemodynamic change indicates postpartum hemorrhage.

items.stem: What is the most likely cause of the bleeding?
items.rationale: A boggy enlarged uterus strongly suggests uterine atony.

items.stem: Which problem is highest priority?
options: Acute blood loss with risk of shock
items.rationale: Ongoing hemorrhage threatens circulation and life.

items.stem: Which interventions belong in the immediate plan?
options: Fundal massage, hemorrhage protocol, IV access/fluids and prescribed uterotonics as appropriate
Give a sedative and dim lights only
items.rationale: Rapid control of uterine bleeding and circulatory support are priorities.

items.stem: What should the nurse do immediately for the boggy uterus?
options: Massage the fundus while summoning/continuing hemorrhage support
Place the client prone and leave the room
Apply a heating pad to the calf
items.rationale: Fundal massage is an immediate action for suspected uterine atony.

items.stem: Which finding best indicates successful early treatment?
options: Uterus becomes firm, bleeding decreases and hemodynamics improve
items.rationale: Reduced bleeding with a firm uterus and improved perfusion indicates response.

items.stem: Which cues are most concerning?
options: Sudden dyspnea, hypoxemia, tachycardia and pleuritic chest pain
items.rationale: The abrupt cardiopulmonary changes are classic warning cues for PE.

items.stem: Which condition best explains the presentation?
items.rationale: The sudden onset and severity after surgery strongly support PE.

items.stem: Which threat is highest priority?
items.rationale: PE can rapidly impair gas exchange and circulation.

items.stem: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Immediate oxygenation/hemodynamic support, urgent provider/rapid response evaluation and prescribed diagnostic/treatment pathway
items.rationale: Possible PE is time-sensitive and requires immediate stabilization and evaluation.

items.stem: What should the nurse do first?
options: Stay with the client, support oxygenation and activate urgent assistance
Offer oral fluids and reassess in two hours
items.rationale: The client is unstable; immediate ABC support and urgent response are required.

items.stem: Which change indicates improvement?
options: SpO2 and work of breathing improve with stable blood pressure
items.rationale: Improved oxygenation, breathing and hemodynamics indicate stabilization.
